progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: see Scope. Students start Year 12 and have watched chem-m5-p02 (Module 5), chem-m8-p02 and chem-m8-c04 in playlist order.
progression.startsWith: Two blue solutions. Your eye can tell which one is darker, but not how much copper is in either. A calibration turns that colour into a number. You measure how much light some solutions of known concentration absorb, draw the line they make, then read a sample you don't know straight off that line. Today you build one for copper, and use it on rinse water from a copper plating workshop.
progression.stopsAfter: stating the aim and variables of a calibration investigation; making standards from a stock by dilution; choosing the wavelength from a scan and zeroing with a blank; handling cuvettes with reasons; plotting the calibration and finding its linear range from the data; diluting an over-range unknown, reading it across then down and multiplying back; judging reliability, accuracy (check standard) and validity; writing the risk rows for copper(II) sulfate, the unknown sample, glassware and the instrument.
progression.nextLesson: calibration and water-analysis data practice (route chem-m8-g02). The route review (change 10) places skills-s06 (graphs and data) before g02 in the Chemistry playlist, so the handoff line names g02 only and the playlist shows s06 between them.

teaching.task: Your eye can rank two blue solutions, but it can't tell you how much copper is in either. How do you make a set of copper(II) standards, turn their absorbances into a calibration line you can trust, and use it to find the copper in a sample you don't know?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) a calibration turns colour into a number (1); (2) the aim, standards defined, the variables (2); (3) standards by dilution with two rinsed burettes (3); (4) the wavelength from a scan, and why the peak; the blank and what it removes (4); (5) cuvette handling, each with its reason (5); (6) plot, the line, the linear range from the bending standard, the slope (6); (7) the unknown above the range, so dilute, not extend; three readings (7); (8) read across then down, then multiply back (8); (9) reliability from repeats; accuracy from a check standard (9); (10) validity: only copper absorbs; same conditions; inside the range (10); (11) hazards and controls, waste (11); memory aid (12); attempts (13 to 16); decision rule and handoff (17); key notes (18).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Two blue solutions. The aim is to find the concentration of copper ions in that rinse water. Start from a stock solution of copper sulfate, point two zero zero moles per litre. Which light? A blue solution absorbs at the red end of the spectrum. Hold each cuvette by its ridged sides, and wipe the clear sides, because a fingerprint scatters light and adds absorbance. Here are the readings. Now the rinse water. Read across from point eight four five to the line, then down: point zero seven one zero moles per litre. Reliable? The three readings agree within about point zero zero six, and a second dilution gives the same answer. Valid? The method measures copper only if copper is the only thing absorbing at that wavelength. Now the risks. Two lines to keep. Your turn. Read across from point three two five, then down: point two five zero moles per litre. Last one. The fingerprint scatters some light, so less reaches the detector, and the absorbance reads high. So, to trust a calibration: make your standards by careful dilution, zero with a blank, and keep the unknown inside the linear range, diluting it if you must.
teaching.openingDecision: Two blue solutions. Your eye can tell which one is darker, but not how much copper is in either. A calibration turns that colour into a number. You measure how much light some solutions of known concentration absorb, draw the line they make, then read a sample you don't know straight off that line. Today you build one for copper, and use it on rinse water from a copper plating workshop.
teaching.understandingCheck: Two, each 10 s with the countdown and every condition visible (13, 15): A1's graph with gridlines, both volumes and the diluted absorbance; A2's clean standards cuvette against the fingerprinted unknown cuvette. Nothing answer-bearing during the holds.

- ultraviolet-visible spectrophotometry
- atomic absorption spectroscopy"

design.visualSystem: no people, hands or faces (filling burettes, pouring, wiping and moving cuvettes are coded motion); apparatus as painted plates listed by filename, never stretched; calibration curves and the wavelength scan are coded lineGraph diagrams, never AI images; at most about three bright text items, earlier lines dim; the calculation as a separate task, equation and grouped givens, one stage at a time; "Pause here to answer." then a 10 s countdown with the full worded question kept on screen; no givens card in the attempts, givens underlined in the feedback as they are used; brief feedback (about 15 to 30 s) with one crossed-out mistake; original HSC-style questions only; real GHS classifications; Australian spelling; no em dashes; conversational narration; no absolute claims; optional key notes hold.
